column5: heart-prayer; moving lips; unheard voice
column6: The commentary joins remembrance on the tongue and in the heart; Hannah prays in her heart, with moving lips but an unheard voice, making an unusually close scriptural scene of inward yet bodily prayer.

column5: Hannah's lips and unheard voice
column6: Berakhot derives prayer rules from Hannah's verse: direct the heart, move the lips, and do not make the voice heard. It gives the commentary's loud/quiet prayer contrast a precise rabbinic liturgical reading.

column5: quiet prayer; God hears the heart
column6: Cyprian teaches that prayer should be quiet because God hears the heart rather than the volume of a voice. This directly interprets the commentary's claim that God knows recitation whether it is on the tongue or in the heart.

column5: secret prayer; Father sees in secret
column6: The commentary pairs inward prayer with God's knowledge of what is concealed; Jesus commands prayer in the shut room, where the Father sees in secret, giving that pair a Christian discipline of prayer.

column5: God searches hearts; Spirit's intention
column6: The commentary says the Lord knows worship that remains inside; Romans names God as the searcher of hearts who knows the Spirit's intention, making divine knowledge the ground of unvoiced intercession.

column5: Jesus knows reasoning within hearts
column6: The commentary's God knows what is hidden as well as what is uttered; Mark's Jesus immediately knows the scribes' inward reasoning, a narrative Christian counterpart focused on concealed thought.

column5: word on tongue already known
column6: The commentary explicitly sets raised speech beside what remains hidden. Psalm 139 says that before a word is on the tongue, YHWH knows it completely, giving the verbal side of that claim its closest Hebrew formulation.

column5: God observes heart and hears tongue
column6: The commentary distinguishes heart and tongue while affirming God's knowledge of both. Wisdom calls God an observer of the heart and a hearer of the tongue, preserving both terms in one ethical warning about speech.

column5: no thought or word hidden
column6: The commentary joins disclosed speech to what stays concealed; Sirach says that no thought escapes God and no word is hidden from him, supplying a compact Jewish formulation of both halves.

column5: secret things and revealed things
column6: The commentary treats hidden and open things as known by God and brought into relation with recited teaching. Deuteronomy assigns secret things to YHWH and revealed things to Israel for doing the Torah, sharpening the disclosure boundary.

column5: God reveals deep and hidden things
column6: The commentary turns concealment into emergence and says God knows the hidden. Daniel's God reveals deep and hidden things, knows what is in darkness, and has light with him, matching both disclosure and light-darkness imagery.

column5: outward appearance and heart
column6: The commentary contrasts what is open with inward reality. In Samuel, humans look at outward appearance while YHWH looks at the heart, a concrete distinction between visible surface and divinely known interior.

column5: YHWH searches heart and tests inward self
column6: The commentary says the hidden interior is known even when no voice exposes it. Jeremiah presents YHWH as searching the heart and testing the inward person, placing that claim in judgment language.

column5: deep things from darkness brought to light
column6: The commentary's second scene makes the concealed come out from its cover. Job says God uncovers deep things from darkness and brings deep shadow into light, a direct divine movement from hiddenness to exposure.

column5: hidden thing brought to light
column6: The commentary uses physical emergence and a cleared well to picture disclosure. Job's mining poem says that a hidden thing is brought to light, supplying a terrestrial extraction image without making the human miner identical with God.

column5: no creature hidden; all exposed to God
column6: The commentary's open/hidden pair is made absolute here: Hebrews says no creature is hidden before God and all stand exposed to his eyes, extending the claim beyond speech to every creature.

column5: hidden darkness and counsels of hearts disclosed
column6: The commentary joins concealed things emerging from cover with the knowledge of inner reality. Paul says the Lord will bring hidden darkness to light and disclose the counsels of hearts, uniting both movements in judgment.

column5: hidden made manifest; secret made known
column6: The commentary describes concealment as capable of becoming visible. Jesus states that nothing hidden will fail to become manifest and no secret will fail to become known and come to light, a close disclosure formula.

column5: YHWH reveals secret to prophets
column6: The commentary frames recited divine speech around what God knows in secret. Amos says the Lord reveals his secret to prophetic servants, adding a biblical account of hidden counsel becoming prophetic proclamation.

column5: mystery hidden through ages now manifested
column6: The commentary makes the hidden something God can bring out. Colossians calls Christ's mystery hidden through ages and generations but now manifested to the saints, a Christian revelation-history form of that movement.

column5: written song taught and put in mouths
column6: The commentary reads 87:6 as recitation from memory or from a text. Deuteronomy orders a song to be written, taught, and put in Israel's mouths, explicitly joining writing, learning, and oral recitation.

column5: song not forgotten from descendants' mouths
column6: The commentary foregrounds the promise of recitation without forgetting. Deuteronomy says the taught song will not be forgotten from descendants' mouths, a close covenantal counterpart to preserved oral memory.

column5: Torah book in mouth and meditation
column6: The commentary joins an uttered reading to an inward one. Joshua requires the Torah book not to depart from the mouth and commands meditation on it day and night, holding oral and interior engagement together.

column5: word stored in heart
column6: The commentary calls recitation possible from the heart. The psalmist says the divine word has been stored or hidden in the heart, turning inward retention into a safeguard for faithful action.

column5: word in mouth and heart
column6: The commentary's central pair is stated almost structurally here: Deuteronomy says the word is very near, in the mouth and in the heart, so that it can be done.

column5: word in mouth and heart
column6: The commentary says the taught word is known whether voiced or held within. Romans reuses the mouth-and-heart formula for the proclaimed word of faith, giving the paired locations a Christ-centered reading.

column5: law placed in mind and written on heart
column6: The commentary's recitation from the heart is not merely silent sound. Hebrews describes God's law placed in minds and written on hearts, a durable inward inscription of revealed teaching.

column5: word dwelling richly; songs in hearts
column6: The commentary connects recitation, remembrance, and worship in tongue and heart. Colossians commands Christ's word to dwell richly and joins teaching with sung worship in hearts, preserving that combined practice.

column5: spoken psalms and melody in heart
column6: The commentary distinguishes audible speech from inward remembrance without separating them. Ephesians pairs speaking psalms and hymns with singing and making melody in the heart to the Lord.

column5: one reads aloud and others hear
column6: The commentary begins with the voice of recitation. Revelation blesses the single reader who reads prophecy aloud together with those who hear it, a specific early Christian scene of voiced scripture.

column5: God's words remain in successive mouths
column6: The commentary treats divine teaching as recited and not forgotten. Isaiah's covenant says God's words will not depart from the prophet's mouth or the mouths of descendants, extending memorized speech through generations.

column5: Arabic q-r-' label; Hebrew qara' reading
column6: The commentary labels the 87:6 reading root q-r-'. Deuteronomy uses the Hebrew cognate qara' for reading the Torah before all Israel in their hearing, showing a Semitic root in an explicitly public reading act.

column5: Arabic dhikr label; Hebrew zkr and God's name
column6: The commentary labels 87:15 with dhikr and has the worshipper remember the Lord's name. Psalm 20 uses Hebrew zkr for Israel's making mention of YHWH's name, a close cognate-and-ritual match.

column5: Arabic dhikr label; Hebrew zikri and divine name
column6: The commentary's dhikr label joins remembrance to the Lord's name. Exodus calls YHWH's declared name his zikri, "my memorial/remembrance," making name and remembrance inseparable in divine self-disclosure.

column5: Hebrew zkr, book of remembrance, and honored name
column6: The commentary's dhikr of the Lord's name is voiced worship. Malachi has God hear those who speak together and honor his name, then records them in a book of remembrance from Hebrew zkr.

column5: calling on the Lord's name
column6: The commentary ends the sequence with remembering the Lord's name and praying. Romans applies the scriptural promise that everyone who calls on the Lord's name will be saved, making invocation of the name a Christian prayer act.

column5: rain makes earth bring forth and sprout
column6: The commentary says rain draws pasture from soil. Isaiah compares rain and snow that water the earth and make it bring forth and sprout, a close image of divinely enabled vegetal emergence.

column5: rainless wasteland satisfied; grass sprouts
column6: The commentary moves from rain and earth to grass coming out. In God's questions to Job, the desolate ground is satisfied so that grass is caused to sprout, placing pasture-growth under divine agency.

column5: God makes grass grow from earth
column6: The commentary links 87:4's bringing out of pasture to divine action. Psalm 104 says God makes grass grow for cattle and vegetation for human service, a direct hymn-like counterpart to that pastoral image.

column5: bright sky-light cannot be seen
column6: The commentary adds the paradox that excessive sunlight can obstruct sight. Job says people cannot see the bright light in the skies, giving a specific biblical instance where brightness defeats vision.

column5: unable to see because of brilliant light
column6: The commentary's cehra image is an eye unable to see in sun. Paul says he could not see because of the brilliance of the heavenly light, a narrative instance of sight overwhelmed by light.

column5: Shema audible to one's own ear
column6: The commentary places elevated and inward recitation together. This Mishnah debates whether a Shema made audible to the reciter's own ear fulfills the duty, giving low but articulated sound a specific legal significance.

column5: wordless groanings in prayer
column6: The commentary allows worship to remain within rather than rise as loud speech. Romans describes the Spirit's intercession through groanings too deep for words, an explicit Christian image of prayer beyond utterance.

column5: communal silence and speech to self and God
column6: The commentary balances voiced and internal devotion. Paul tells an uninterpreted speaker to keep silence in the assembly while speaking to himself and to God, distinguishing public sound from God-directed speech.

column5: God knows needs before spoken prayer
column6: The commentary says God knows an inward as well as uttered reading. Augustine explains that prayer-words do not inform God, who already knows human need, but exercise the pray-er’s desire; this is a patristic account of the same premise.

column5: seed sprouts and grows without the sower's knowing
column6: The commentary makes hiddenness a process of emergence, especially grass from earth. Jesus' seed sprouts and grows while the sower does not know how, setting hidden vegetal growth beside the commentary's divine knowing.

column5: opened eyes and a seen well of water
column6: The commentary uses a cleared, visible well as an image of disclosure. God opens Hagar's eyes and she sees a well of water, making hidden provision visible without claiming that the well itself was newly created.

column5: covered under wings and feathers
column6: The commentary's hawafi are feathers hidden below the leading wing-feathers. Psalm 91 pictures protection under God's wings and feathers, offering a concrete feather-cover image while giving it a protective sense.

column5: chicks gathered under a bird's wings
column6: The commentary uses concealed lesser feathers beneath a wing. Jesus' hen image gathers chicks under wings, another bird-cover scene whose protective purpose adds a relational use of the concealed space.

column5: shining face covered by a veil
column6: The commentary says excess light can itself become a covering. Exodus combines Moses' shining face with his putting on a veil, a biblical scene in which radiance and covering are deliberately held together.

column5: fire followed by a sound of thin silence
column6: The commentary connects volume, concealment, and the Qur'anic approach to Moses' fire. After fire, Elijah's Horeb scene contains qol demamah daqqah, a "sound of thin silence," an indirect but unusually apt acoustic counter-image.

column5: Moses and fire in the bush
column6: The commentary locates the Qur'anic loud/hidden saying immediately before Moses sees fire. Exodus likewise gives Moses a fire-theophany, though specifically a bush burning without being consumed, so the shared scene and its differing detail can be compared.

column5: God calls Moses from the bush
column6: The commentary's nearby Qur'anic setting moves from divine knowledge of speech to the Moses-fire encounter. Exodus 3:4 contributes the verbal side within its own verse: God calls Moses by name from the bush.
